cards.title: Roberto Busa
cards.body: A Jesuit whose 1946 doctorate chased the idea of presence in Thomas Aquinas. The word that carried it turned out to be a preposition, in, so he needed every function word, everywhere, across ten million words of medieval Latin. In 1949 he crossed America asking universities for a machine that could help.
cards.prompt: In 1949 a Jesuit went looking for machinery to finish something he had already started by hand. What was he trying to build, and what had the hand attempt already cost him?
cards.answer: A complete concordance of Thomas Aquinas — every word, function words included, mapped to every place it occurs. For his doctorate he had already written out 10,000 cards by hand, one sentence each, for a single preposition.

cards.title: The meeting a report on Watson's desk had already vetoed
cards.sub: 1949 · IBM, New York · recalled by Busa in 1980
cards.body: Busa arrived at IBM with no funding and a proposal that a report on Watson's desk already called impossible. He left with IBM's machines committed to a medieval Latin text and Paul Tasman assigned to work with him. The whole arrangement rested on a slogan and a handshake.
cards.prompt: A report on Watson's desk said IBM machines could never do it. What did Busa put in front of Thomas J. Watson Sr. to turn that around, and what price did IBM ask?
cards.answer: IBM's own waiting-room poster: 'The difficult we do right away; the impossible takes a little longer.' Watson agreed IBM would cooperate until the project was completed, on one condition — 'provided that you do not change IBM into International Busa Machines.' Busa had already told him he could recompense IBM in any way except financially.

cards.title: The sample volume that proved a machine had done it
cards.body: The first thing the collaboration shipped was not the index. It was a proof: a small concordance of one narrow corpus, printed straight off punched cards and laid on a table at a documentation conference in Rome so people could see that a machine, not a monk, had compiled it.
cards.prompt: Two years in, one thin volume was exhibited in Rome to show the method worked. Name it, and say what its subtitle claimed to be a first of.
cards.answer: S. Thomae Aquinatis Hymnorum Ritualium: Varia Specimina Concordantiarum (Milano: Bocca, 1951), subtitled 'A First Example of a Word Index Automatically Compiled and Printed by IBM Punched Card Machines', exhibited at the XVIII World Conference of Documentation.

cards.title: Term, then the sorted list of places
cards.sub: 1980 · Busa's own accounting of thirty years
cards.body: Sort a deck of one-word cards and you have manufactured a map from term to locations. Lucene, Elasticsearch and every code-search engine store that same map. Busa's numbers say where it costs: fewer than 10,000 computer hours against more than a million man hours, a ratio above 100 to 1.
cards.prompt: Busa built an inverted index with no computer, which makes two of its costs impossible to hide. Name both — the ones no amount of query tuning removes.
cards.answer: One: the index is a separate artifact, built and sorted offline from the documents, so freshness is a build problem rather than a query problem. Two: the analyzer's ruling on what counts as one term is frozen into the artifact, so changing it means rebuilding the whole thing.
